title: Rates of Reaction

cards.b: Petrol burns in a flash; iron rusts over years; diamonds last forever, even though graphite is more stable. Chemical kinetics studies how fast reactions go and why. Controlling speed is the heart of cooking, medicine shelf-life and industrial profit.

For particles to react they must collide, with enough energy and in the right orientation. Most collisions fail, like trying to snap a stick with a gentle tap.

The minimum energy needed is the activation energy. Svante Arrhenius (1889) showed how rate depends on it: lower activation energy or higher temperature means a faster reaction.

Imagine pushing a boulder over a hill before it rolls down. The hill is the activation energy.

Even an exothermic reaction needs this push. A match gives the initial energy for paper to burn.

cards.h: Four ways to speed up a reaction
cards.b:
• Higher concentration (or pressure for gases): more collisions per second.
  • Higher temperature: more particles exceed the activation energy. A rough rule: the rate roughly doubles for each 10 °C rise.
  • Greater surface area: powdered solids react faster than lumps. Flour dust can explode.
  • Catalyst: see below.

A catalyst gives the reaction an easier path with lower activation energy and is not used up. It does not change the final products or amount.

  • Iron in the Haber process.
  • Vanadium pentoxide in making sulphuric acid.
  • Platinum, palladium and rhodium in car catalytic converters, which convert CO and NOx into CO2 and N2.
  • Enzymes: biological catalysts, e.g. amylase in saliva.

The rate is how fast concentration changes: rate = change in concentration / time. For a first-order reaction, the rate is proportional to the concentration, and the time for the quantity to halve, the half-life, is constant.

Radioactive decay follows this pattern, as do many drug breakdowns in the body.

A reaction has half-life 10 minutes. Start with 80 g. After 30 minutes?

30 / 10 = 3 half-lives: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 g.

Rate: concentration falls from 0.50 mol/L to 0.20 mol/L in 15 s. Average rate = 0.30 / 15 = 0.02 mol/L per second.

• Catalysts are not consumed and do not shift the equilibrium.
  • Exothermic does not mean fast. Activation energy decides speed.
  • Heating speeds all reactions (it increases particles with enough energy), but enzymes stop working if overheated.
  • Half-life is not half of the time to complete; it never fully reaches zero in theory.

India moved to Bharat Stage VI emission norms nationwide in April 2020, leaping from BS-IV. Cleaner petrol and diesel plus better catalytic converters and particulate filters cut sulphur and tailpipe pollutants sharply. The converter is a catalyst: tiny platinum-group metal particles on a honeycomb speed up the conversion of CO and NOx into harmless gases.

• Reactions need collisions with energy above the activation energy.
  • Faster with higher concentration, temperature, surface area and catalysts.
  • Half-life: quantity halves each constant time period.
